newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA RELEASES DRAFT LAW TO STOP LAND EVICTIONS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA RELEASES DRAFT LAW TO STOP LAND EVICTIONS.

text.p: South Africa on Wednesday published draft legislation to stop unfair land evictions, a fate that yearly befalls thousands of mainly black farmworkers and tenants living on white-owned land.
Geoff Budlender, director general of land affairs, said the proposed Bill, which is expected to be passed this year, would make it more difficult to push occupants off land.
But the South African Agricultural Union (SAAU) criticised the draft document for giving the state "extraordinary and unacceptable powers" to interfere in tenant-owner relations.
It said the move could harm South Africa's agricultural competitiveness.
Millions of blacks, impoverished by racist laws that chased them off large tracts of land and prevented them from owning property in certain areas, live on land belonging to other people.
Following the first democratic elections in 1994, the black-led government has twice called for a moratorium on evictions but Budlender said there had been no legal way to enforce this on landowners.
"Now evictions can only take place by a court order," he said.
Although the proposed Bill allowed lawful evictions, for reasons including refusal to pay rent, a court would have to consider whether an eviction was fair and justified under the circumstances.
Once this had been established, eviction could not take place until adequate alternative accommodation was available.
This would be subsidised by government through either the Land Affairs Department's land acquisition or a settlement grant or through a housing subsidy.
Subsidies would be funded out of the Land Department's redistribution programme which had a budget of 300 million rand ($66 million) next year.
"The money is there...in future we may need more. The important thing is putting it to use," Budlender told Reuters.
He said the Bill was aimed at striking a balance between giving effective protection and tenure security to land occupiers, while recognising the legitimate interests of land-owners.
But the SAAU said the document created confusion and uncertainty.

"South African agriculture must compete internationally and legislation which over-regulates the situation on the farm and which has cost implications for farmers could impact negatively on such competitiveness and food production," Pieter Erasmus, the chairman of the sAAU's labour committee, said.
The four main principles contained in the proposed Bill are:
- people who live on land which belongs to others should, subject to reasonable limitations, be guaranteed basic human rights, including freedom of movement and association;
- the law should prevent unfair and arbitrary evictions;
- it should promote long-term land security with government assisting owners and occupiers to find this solution; and
- existing rights of ownership should be recognised.
Current laws, including the Prevention of Illegal Squatting Act of 1951 and the Trespass Act of 1959 which are contrary to the Constitution and the proposed Bill, will be amended.
